title: Probability theory, Bayes and Naive Bayes

cards.question: Why do ML algorithms often work with the probability that an image belongs to a category, rather than only the discrete event that it does?
cards.answer: The probability is a continuous quantity, and continuous quantities are easier to optimize than discrete events.
distractors: Probabilities are always exactly 0 or 1, which makes every decision unambiguous.
Probabilities remove all uncertainty from the data.
Probabilities make the model independent of the training data.

cards.question: Pragmatically, what role does probability theory play in AI and machine learning?
cards.answer: It is the formal framework for dealing with uncertainty and incomplete information.
distractors: It is a method for reducing the dimension of high-dimensional data.
It is a distance measure used to compare data objects.
It guarantees that a model never makes mistakes on unseen data.

cards.question: What does P(A|B) = x express?
cards.answer: The degree of belief that A is true, given that B is accepted as true, is at level x, a number between 0 and 1.
distractors: The fraction of all experiments in which A and B occur together, regardless of what is known.
The probability that B is true given that A is accepted as true.
The correlation between A and B, a number between -1 and 1.

cards.question: In the course's framework, what kind of statements are A and B in P(A|B), and what do probabilities represent?
cards.answer: A and B are always binary (true/false) propositions, and the probability represents a state of knowledge.
distractors: A and B are real-valued variables, and the probability represents a physical property of the world.
A and B are always continuous quantities, and the probability represents a measured frequency.
A and B are class labels, and the probability represents a distance between them.

cards.question: In the trial example, G = 'the accused is guilty' and E = E1 and E2 and E3 collects three pieces of evidence. What does P(G|E) > P(G|E2) illustrate?
cards.answer: Probabilities express states of knowledge: conditioning on more evidence changes the plausibility of G.
distractors: Probabilities are fixed properties of the accused and cannot change with evidence.
Evidence E2 on its own is always stronger than all the evidence combined.
Conditional probabilities must always be smaller than unconditional ones.

cards.question: In propositional notation, what does the product AB mean?
cards.answer: The proposition that is true when A and B are both true.
distractors: The proposition that is true when either A or B is true.
The proposition that is true when A is false.
The proposition that is true when exactly one of A and B is true.

cards.question: In propositional notation, what does A + B mean, and what does the bar in A-bar mean?
cards.answer: A + B is true if either A or B is true, and A-bar is true if A is false.
distractors: A + B is true only if both are true, and A-bar is true if A is true.
A + B is true if exactly one of them is true, and A-bar is the probability of A.
A + B is the probability of A plus the probability of B, and A-bar is the conditional probability of A.

cards.question: What are the special propositions '1' and '0', and what does the shorthand P(A|1) = P(A) say?
cards.answer: 1 is a proposition that is always true and 0 one that is always false; conditioning on 1 means conditioning on no extra knowledge, which gives the plain probability P(A).
distractors: 1 and 0 are the probabilities of A and A-bar; P(A|1) = P(A) says the two sum to 1.
1 is the event that A happens once and 0 that it never happens; P(A|1) = P(A) holds only for binary A.
1 and 0 are the values a Bernoulli variable can take; P(A|1) = P(A) says the variable equals 1.

cards.question: What is the sum rule of probability?
cards.answer: P(A|C) + P(A-bar|C) = 1.
distractors: P(A|C) + P(A|C-bar) = 1.
P(A|C) * P(A-bar|C) = 1.

cards.question: What is the product rule of probability?
cards.answer: P(AB|C) = P(B|AC) P(A|C) = P(A|BC) P(B|C).
distractors: P(AB|C) = P(A|C) + P(B|C).
P(AB|C) = P(A|BC) P(A|C).
P(AB|C) = P(B|AC) / P(A|C).

cards.question: What is the interpretation of P(A|B) = 0 and of P(A|B) = 1?
cards.answer: P(A|B) = 0 means that given B is true, A is certainly false; P(A|B) = 1 means that given B is true, A is certainly true.
distractors: P(A|B) = 0 means A is impossible in general; P(A|B) = 1 means B is certainly true.
P(A|B) = 0 means A and B are independent; P(A|B) = 1 means A and B are identical events.
P(A|B) = 0 means B is certainly false; P(A|B) = 1 means B is certainly true.

cards.question: How does Bayes' theorem follow from the product rule?
cards.answer: Since P(AB) = P(A|B)P(B) = P(B|A)P(A), we get P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A) / P(B).
distractors: Since P(AB) = P(A) + P(B), we get P(A|B) = P(B|A) + P(A) - P(B).
Since P(A|B) + P(A-bar|B) = 1, we get P(A|B) = 1 - P(B|A).
Since P(AB) = P(A)P(B), we get P(A|B) = P(B|A).

cards.question: How can P(B|C) be written by marginalizing over A, using the sum and product rules?
cards.answer: P(B|C) = P(B|AC) P(A|C) + P(B|A-bar C) P(A-bar|C).
distractors: P(B|C) = P(B|AC) P(A|C) - P(B|A-bar C) P(A-bar|C).
P(B|C) = P(B|AC) + P(B|A-bar C).
P(B|C) = P(A|BC) P(B|C) + P(A-bar|BC) P(B|C).

cards.question: What is the expanded form of Bayes' theorem for P(A|BC) that includes the marginalization in the denominator?
cards.answer: P(A|BC) = P(B|AC)P(A|C) / [P(B|AC)P(A|C) + P(B|A-bar C)P(A-bar|C)].
distractors: P(A|BC) = P(B|AC)P(A|C) / [P(B|AC) + P(B|A-bar C)].
P(A|BC) = P(B|AC)P(A|C) / [P(A|BC)P(B|C) + P(A-bar|BC)P(B|C)].
P(A|BC) = [P(B|AC) + P(A|C)] / P(B|C).

cards.question: When are events A1, ..., An mutually exclusive, and what is P(A1 + ... + An) in that case?
cards.answer: When no two can be true at the same time (AiAj = 0 for i != j); then P(A1 + ... + An) = the sum of the P(Ai).
distractors: When at least one of them must be true; then the sum of the P(Ai) equals 1.
When they are independent; then P(A1 + ... + An) = the product of the P(Ai).
When they cover all outcomes; then P(A1 + ... + An) = 0.

cards.question: For two events that are not necessarily mutually exclusive, what is P(A + B)?
cards.answer: P(A) + P(B) - P(AB).
distractors: P(A) + P(B).
P(A) P(B).
P(A) + P(B) + P(AB).

cards.question: A die gives events A1, ..., A6, where Ai means 'side i is face up'. What is the relation between these events?
cards.answer: They are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so their probabilities sum to 1.
distractors: They are independent and exhaustive, so their probabilities multiply to 1.
They are mutually exclusive but not exhaustive, since a die could land on an edge.
They are exhaustive but not mutually exclusive, since several sides can face up together.

cards.question: R1, R2, R3 mean 'handed in report 1, 2, 3' and F means 'failed 02450'. How do you express 'if a student hands in reports 1, 2 and 3, the chance of passing is greater than 90%'?
cards.answer: P(not F | R1 R2 R3) > 0.9, since passing is not failing and the reports are the evidence being conditioned on.
distractors: P(R1 R2 R3 | F) > 0.9, which asks how likely a failing student handed in everything.
P(F | R1 R2 R3) > 0.9, which says the student is likely to fail.
P(not F | R1 + R2 + R3) > 0.9, which only requires at least one report.

cards.question: Why are stochastic (random) variables useful compared with reasoning directly with events?
cards.answer: Complicated questions would require logic and counting over events; random variables let us manipulate the quantities with algebra and general formulas.
distractors: They guarantee that every probability becomes exactly 0 or 1.
They remove the need for the sum rule and the product rule.
They allow us to avoid ever specifying a distribution.

cards.question: What is the event X_x and what does the random variable notation P(X = x) = p(x) express?
cards.answer: X_x is the binary event that X equals the number x; P(X = x) = p(x) is its probability written in random variable notation.
distractors: X_x is the event that X is at least x; p(x) is the cumulative probability up to x.
X_x is the average of X over x observations; p(x) is its variance.
X_x is the proposition that X is true; p(x) is a density that can exceed 1.

cards.question: How do the sum and product rules look for discrete random variables?
cards.answer: Sum rule: sum over i of p(x_i|z_k) = 1; product rule: p(x_i, y_j|z_k) = p(x_i|y_j, z_k) p(y_j|z_k).
distractors: Sum rule: p(x_i|z_k) + p(y_j|z_k) = 1; product rule: p(x_i, y_j|z_k) = p(x_i|z_k) + p(y_j|z_k).
Sum rule: sum over i of p(x_i|z_k) = 0; product rule: p(x_i, y_j|z_k) = p(x_i|y_j, z_k) / p(y_j|z_k).
Sum rule: sum over k of p(x_i|z_k) = 1; product rule: p(x_i, y_j|z_k) = p(x_i|z_k) p(y_j|x_i).

cards.question: Roll a die N times. How do you model the number of sixes using random variables?
cards.answer: Let X_i be a Bernoulli(1/6) variable that is 1 if roll i is a six; the number of sixes X = X_1 + ... + X_N is Binomial(N, 1/6).
distractors: Let X_i be Bernoulli(1/6) and take X = X_1 * X_2 * ... * X_N, which is Binomial(N, 1/6).
Let X_i be Bernoulli(5/6) and take X to be the largest X_i.
Count the 6^N outcomes and enumerate those with K sixes directly; this is the only option.

cards.question: What is the Bernoulli distribution for a binary variable b with parameter theta?
cards.answer: p(b|theta) = theta^b (1 - theta)^(1-b), so p(b=1|theta) = theta and p(b=0|theta) = 1 - theta.
distractors: p(b|theta) = theta^(1-b) (1 - theta)^b, so p(b=1|theta) = 1 - theta.
p(b|theta) = theta * b, so p(b=1|theta) = theta and p(b=0|theta) = 0.
p(b|theta) = (1 - theta)^b, so p(b=0|theta) = theta.

cards.question: In the Bernoulli distribution, what role does the parameter theta play?
cards.answer: It determines the probability that the random variable takes the value 1, and lies in the interval [0, 1].
distractors: It is the expected number of trials before the first success.
It is the variance of the binary variable and can be any positive number.
It is the number of times the binary event is repeated.

cards.question: What is the distribution of the sum of N independent Bernoulli(theta) variables, and what is P(X = k)?
cards.answer: Binomial(N, theta), with P(X = k) = C(N, k) theta^k (1 - theta)^(N - k).
distractors: Gaussian(N theta, N), with P(X = k) given by a density.
Bernoulli(N theta), with P(X = k) = theta^k (1 - theta)^(1-k).
Binomial(N, theta), with P(X = k) = theta^k (1 - theta)^k.

cards.question: A fair die is rolled 3 times. What is the probability of exactly two sixes?
distractors: 5/216, which counts only one arrangement of the two sixes.
1/36, which ignores the third roll.
25/72, which is the probability of exactly one six.

cards.question: The red bowl holds 5 oranges and 2 apples, and the blue bowl holds 1 orange and 4 apples. What is the probability of an orange if the bowl is red?
In the same bowls (red: 5 oranges, 2 apples; blue: 1 orange, 4 apples), what is the probability of the red bowl if the fruit is an orange?
Why do p(orange | red bowl) = 5/7 and p(red bowl | orange) = 5/6 differ, and how are they linked?
cards.answer: They condition on different things (the bowl versus the fruit); Bayes' theorem links them: p(r|o) = p(o|r)p(r)/p(o).
distractors: They differ because of a counting mistake; both must equal the joint probability 5/12.
They differ only because the bowls have different sizes, and Bayes' theorem does not link them.
They are linked by p(r|o) = p(o|r) + p(r) - p(o).

cards.question: With 12 pieces of fruit (5 oranges and 2 apples in the red bowl), how is p(r) = 7/12 obtained from the joint probabilities?
cards.answer: By marginalization: p(r) = p(r, o=0) + p(r, o=1) = 2/12 + 5/12.
distractors: By the product rule: p(r) = p(r|o) p(o) = 5/6 * 6/12.
By Bayes' theorem: p(r) = p(o|r) p(o) / p(r).
By adding the conditionals: p(r) = 5/7 + 2/7.

cards.question: A test detects a disease 99% of the time, gives a false positive 2% of the time, and 1% of the population has the disease. You test positive. What is the probability you have the disease?
In the disease-test example, what is the overall probability of a positive test, p(Positive)?
distractors: 0.0099, which counts only the true positives.
0.0198, which counts only the false positives.
0.99, which is the sensitivity of the test.

cards.question: Why is the posterior probability of disease only 1/3 after a positive test with 99% sensitivity?
cards.answer: The disease is rare (1% prior), so false positives from the large healthy group (about 1.98% of people) outnumber true positives (about 0.99%).
distractors: The test is only 33% accurate on diseased people.
The probability of a false positive is higher than the probability of a true positive.
Bayes' theorem always divides a probability by three when there are two hypotheses.

cards.question: In the disease-test example, which quantity is the likelihood and which is the prior in p(Disease|Positive) = p(Positive|Disease) p(Disease) / p(Positive)?
cards.answer: p(Positive|Disease) = 0.99 is the likelihood of the test result, and p(Disease) = 0.01 is the prior.
distractors: p(Disease) = 0.01 is the likelihood, and p(Positive|Disease) = 0.99 is the prior.
p(Positive) is the likelihood, and p(Disease|Positive) is the prior.
p(Positive|NoDisease) = 0.02 is the prior, and p(NoDisease) is the likelihood.

cards.question: 17.5% of customers are from Lisbon, 10.7% from Oporto, 71.8% from Other. The shares spending above the median on delicatessen are 44.1%, 48.9% and 51.6%. What is P(Lisbon | DELI above median)?
cards.answer: About 15.4%.
distractors: About 7.7%, the joint probability P(DELI above median and Lisbon).
44.1%, the probability P(DELI above median | Lisbon).
50.0%, the overall probability of spending above the median.

cards.question: In the delicatessen quiz, how is the denominator P(DELI above median) obtained?
cards.answer: By marginalizing over the cities: sum over cities of P(DELI above median | city) P(city), which is 0.5.
distractors: By taking the largest of the three conditional probabilities, 0.516.
By averaging the three conditional probabilities without weighting by city size.
By multiplying the three conditional probabilities.

cards.question: When are two random variables X and Y independent?
cards.answer: When p(x_i, y_j) = p(x_i) p(y_j) for all values.
distractors: When p(x_i, y_j) = p(x_i) + p(y_j).
When p(x_i | y_j) = p(y_j | x_i).
When p(x_i, y_j) = 0 for all i != j.

cards.question: What does it mean that X and Y are conditionally independent given Z?
cards.answer: p(x_i, y_j | z_k) = p(x_i | z_k) p(y_j | z_k): once z_k is known, the joint probability factorizes.
distractors: p(x_i, y_j) = p(x_i) p(y_j) holds unconditionally, so Z is irrelevant.
p(x_i | y_j, z_k) = p(y_j | x_i, z_k).
p(x_i, y_j | z_k) = p(x_i, y_j) p(z_k).

cards.question: How is the expectation of a function f of a discrete random variable defined?
cards.answer: E[f] = sum over i of f(x_i) p(x_i).
distractors: E[f] = sum over i of f(x_i) / p(x_i).
E[f] = max over i of f(x_i) p(x_i).
E[f] = f(sum over i of x_i p(x_i)) for every f.

cards.question: How are the mean and the variance of a discrete random variable defined?
cards.answer: Mean: E[x] = sum of x_i p(x_i); variance: Var[x] = sum of (x_i - E[x])^2 p(x_i).
distractors: Mean: sum of p(x_i); variance: sum of x_i^2.
Mean: E[x] = sum of x_i / p(x_i); variance: sum of (x_i - E[x]) p(x_i).
Mean: the value with the highest p(x_i); variance: the largest (x_i - E[x]).

cards.question: If all N values are equally likely, p(x_i) = 1/N, what do the expectation formulas reduce to?
cards.answer: E[x] is the ordinary average (sum of x_i)/N, and Var[x] = (1/N) sum of (x_i - E[x])^2.
distractors: E[x] = 1/N, and Var[x] = 1/N^2.
E[x] = sum of x_i, and Var[x] = sum of (x_i - E[x])^2.
E[x] = the median, and Var[x] = (1/(N-1)) sum of x_i^2.

cards.question: How is the expectation of g(x) defined for a continuous random variable with density p(x)?
cards.answer: E[g] = the integral of g(x) p(x) dx.
distractors: E[g] = the sum of g(x) p(x) over all real x.
E[g] = the integral of g(x) dx.
E[g] = g evaluated at the point where p(x) = 1.

cards.question: How are the covariance and the standard deviation defined with expectations?
cards.answer: cov(x, y) = E[(x - E[x])(y - E[y])], and std(x) = sqrt(var(x)), where var(x) = cov(x, x).
distractors: cov(x, y) = E[xy] + E[x]E[y], and std(x) = var(x)^2.
cov(x, y) = E[x - y], and std(x) = E[(x - E[x])].
cov(x, y) = E[(x - E[x])^2], and std(x) = E[x].

cards.question: Why can we not talk about the probability that the rainfall is exactly 2.3 mm?
cards.answer: Rainfall is continuous, so any single exact value has probability zero; only intervals such as 1 to 2 mm have meaningful probabilities.
distractors: Because rainfall values above 2 mm are forbidden by the density.
Because the density at 2.3 mm is always negative.
Because rainfall is discrete and 2.3 is not one of the possible values.

cards.question: For a continuous variable with density p(x), how is the probability of the event 'x lies between a and b' computed?
cards.answer: As the integral of p(x) dx from a to b: the events are intervals, the probability is the integral, and the curve is the density.
distractors: As p(b) - p(a), the difference of the density values at the end points.
As the average of p(a) and p(b).
As the height of the density curve at the midpoint of the interval.

cards.question: The rainfall density is about 0.3 at x = 1 mm. What is the approximate probability of rainfall between 1 and 1.1 mm?
cards.answer: About 0.03, since P(A[x, x+dx]) is approximately p(x) dx = 0.3 * 0.1.
distractors: About 0.3, the value of the density.
About 0.003, since dx should be 0.01.
About 0.1, the width of the interval.

cards.question: How is the probability that a pair of continuous variables (x, y) lies in a region D defined?
cards.answer: As the double integral of the joint density p(x, y) dx dy over the region D.
distractors: As p(x) times p(y), evaluated at the center of D.
As the maximum of p(x, y) over D.
As the single integral of p(x) dx over D.

cards.question: For densities, what are the sum rule and the product rule?
cards.answer: Sum rule: the integral of p(x|z) dx = 1; product rule: p(x, y|z) = p(y|x, z) p(x|z).
distractors: Sum rule: p(x|z) + p(x-bar|z) = 1 as a sum of two densities; product rule: p(x, y|z) = p(x|z) + p(y|z).
Sum rule: p(x|z) integrates to z; product rule: p(x, y|z) = p(y|x, z) / p(x|z).
Sum rule: the sum over x of p(x|z) = 1 and cannot involve integrals; product rule: p(x, y|z) = p(y|z).

cards.question: How does Bayes' theorem look for continuous x?
cards.answer: p(x|y, z) = p(y|x, z) p(x|z) / the integral of p(y|x', z) p(x'|z) dx'.
distractors: p(x|y, z) = p(y|x, z) p(x|z) / the sum over x' of p(y|x', z) without any integral.
p(x|y, z) = p(y|x, z) + p(x|z) minus the integral of p(y|x', z) dx'.
p(x|y, z) = p(x|z) / the integral of p(y|x', z) dx'.

cards.question: How does marginalization differ between discrete and continuous variables?
cards.answer: Discrete: sum over c of p(x = c, y|z) = p(y|z); continuous: the integral of p(x, y|z) dx = p(y|z).
distractors: Discrete: product over c of p(x = c, y|z); continuous: the derivative of p(x, y|z).
Discrete: integral over c; continuous: sum over x.
Both use a sum, since integrals are not allowed for probability densities.

cards.question: What is the density of the multivariate normal distribution N(x | mu, Sigma) for M-dimensional x?
distractors: 1 / (2 pi)^M * exp(-(x - mu)^T (x - mu)), without the covariance matrix.
exp(-1/2 (x - mu)^T Sigma^(-1) (x - mu)), without any normalization constant.

cards.question: What does the multivariate normal density reduce to for M = 1?
cards.answer: 1 / sqrt(2 pi sigma^2) * exp(-(x - mu)^2 / (2 sigma^2)).
distractors: 1 / (2 pi sigma^2) * exp(-(x - mu) / sigma).
sigma / sqrt(2 pi) * exp(-(x - mu)^2 / 2).
1 / sqrt(2 pi) * exp(-(x - mu)^2 * sigma^2 / 2).

cards.question: What do the parameters mu and Sigma of the multivariate normal represent?
cards.answer: mu = E[x] is the mean vector, and Sigma is the covariance matrix with Sigma_ij = cov[x_i, x_j].
distractors: mu is the standard deviation vector, and Sigma is the correlation matrix with ones on the diagonal.
mu is the mode of the first attribute only, and Sigma is the identity matrix scaled by the mean.
mu is the covariance matrix, and Sigma is the mean vector.

cards.question: What properties does a covariance matrix of a normal distribution have?
cards.answer: It is symmetric, has positive values on the diagonal (the variances), and is positive definite (eigenvalues greater than 0).
distractors: It is antisymmetric, with zeros on the diagonal, and has negative eigenvalues.
It is diagonal, with identical values on the diagonal, and has eigenvalues equal to 1.
It is symmetric, with ones on the diagonal, and has eigenvalues that may be negative.

cards.question: For a 2D normal distribution, what do the entries of Sigma contain?
cards.answer: The diagonal holds var(x1) and var(x2), and both off-diagonal entries hold cov[x1, x2].
distractors: The diagonal holds cov[x1, x2] and the off-diagonal entries hold the variances.
The diagonal holds the means of x1 and x2, and the off-diagonal entries hold their correlation.
The first row holds var(x1) and var(x2), and the second row holds the means.

cards.question: What do the contour lines of a 2D normal with Sigma = [[1, 0], [0, 1]] look like?
cards.answer: Circles centered at the mean, because the variances are equal and the covariance is zero.
distractors: Ellipses elongated along the diagonal x1 = x2.
Ellipses elongated along the x1 axis only.
Straight lines through the mean.

cards.question: A 2D normal has Sigma = [[1, 0.9], [0.9, 1]]. What do its contours look like?
cards.answer: Narrow ellipses elongated along the diagonal x1 = x2, because the attributes are strongly positively correlated.
distractors: Circles, because both variances are 1.
Narrow ellipses elongated along the anti-diagonal, because the covariance is large.
Axis-aligned ellipses, because the variances are equal.

cards.question: Three contour plots show a circle (A), a moderately tilted ellipse (B) and a very narrow tilted ellipse (C). All variances are 1 and x1, x2 are positively correlated. Which covariance matrices match A and C?
Why is [[1, -0.45], [0.45, 1]] not a valid covariance matrix for the contour plots in the quiz?
cards.answer: A covariance matrix must be symmetric, and this matrix is not; it also has the wrong sign for the positively correlated plot.
distractors: Its diagonal entries must be 0.
Its determinant must be exactly 1.
A covariance matrix must have all off-diagonal entries equal to 0.

cards.question: What is the Bayes classifier's expression for the class posterior p(y|x1, x2) in a two-class problem?
cards.answer: p(y|x1, x2) = p(x1, x2|y) p(y) / sum over k of p(x1, x2|y = k) p(y = k).

cards.question: In the Bayes classifier, which quantities are the class posterior, the class prior, and the class-conditional distribution?
cards.answer: p(y|x) is the posterior, p(y) is the prior, and p(x|y) is the class-conditional distribution of the attributes.
distractors: p(x|y) is the posterior, p(y) is the prior, and p(y|x) is the class-conditional distribution.
p(y) is the posterior, p(x) is the prior, and p(x|y) is the evidence.
p(x) is the posterior, p(y|x) is the prior, and p(y) is the class-conditional distribution.

cards.question: Training data (gender y: 0 male, 1 female; tall x1, heavy x2): males (1,1), (1,1), (1,1), (0,1); females (1,1), (0,1), (0,0), (0,0). What is P(y=0 | x1=0, x2=1) for a short, heavy person with the full Bayes classifier?
cards.answer: 1/2, since p(0,1|male) = 1/4, p(0,1|female) = 1/4 and the priors are both 4/8.
distractors: 1/4, the class-conditional probability p(0,1|male).
3/4, the fraction of males that are tall.
1/8, the joint probability of male and (0,1).

cards.question: What is the practical problem with estimating p(x1, ..., xM | y = k) by counting in the Bayes classifier?
cards.answer: It requires, for each class, enough observations matching each exact combination of attribute values; the number of combinations grows quickly with M, so most combinations are never observed.
distractors: The counts always sum to more than 1, so the probabilities cannot be normalized.
The class prior p(y) cannot be estimated from data.
The counting only works for continuous attributes.

cards.question: What is the Naive Bayes assumption?
cards.answer: The attributes are conditionally independent given the class: p(x1, ..., xM | y) = p(x1|y) p(x2|y) ... p(xM|y).
distractors: The attributes are independent of each other and of the class: p(x1, ..., xM) = p(x1) ... p(xM).
The class is independent of the attributes: p(y|x1, ..., xM) = p(y).
The attributes are identical given the class: x1 = x2 = ... = xM.

cards.question: What is the Naive Bayes classifier for the class posterior?
cards.answer: p(y|x1, ..., xM) = p(x1|y) ... p(xM|y) p(y) / sum over k of p(x1|y=k) ... p(xM|y=k) p(y=k).

cards.question: Using the same data, what does Naive Bayes give for P(y=1 | x1=1, x2=1), the probability that a tall, heavy person is female?
distractors: 1/4, the posterior from the full joint distribution.
1/2, the prior of the class female.
2/3, the fraction of tall people that are female.

cards.question: For the tall, heavy person, the full Bayes classifier gives P(female) = 1/4 while Naive Bayes gives 1/7. What does the difference show?
cards.answer: Naive Bayes can give different results from the full Bayes classifier when the attributes are not truly conditionally independent given the class.
distractors: One of the two calculations must contain an arithmetic error, since both use the same data.
Naive Bayes always gives a smaller posterior than the full Bayes classifier.
The full Bayes classifier ignores the prior, which causes the difference.

cards.question: In Naive Bayes, what does the product of the factors p(x_j|y) have to be divided by to obtain a proper posterior?
cards.answer: The sum over all classes k of the same product with the prior, so that the posteriors sum to 1.
distractors: The number of attributes M.
The prior p(y) of the predicted class only.
The largest single factor p(x_j|y).

cards.question: For binary attributes, how does the robust (smoothed) Naive Bayes estimate p(x_j = 1 | y = c)?
cards.answer: (n + alpha) / (N_c + 2 alpha), where n is the count of x_j = 1 within class c and N_c the number of class-c observations.
distractors: n / (N_c + alpha), which only adjusts the denominator.
(n + alpha) / (N_c + alpha), which adds alpha once in the denominator.
(n + alpha) / (N + 2 alpha), where N is the total dataset size.

cards.question: For a categorical attribute with K categories, how is p(x_j = k | y = c) estimated robustly?
cards.answer: (n + alpha) / (N_c + K alpha), where n is the number of class-c observations with x_j = k.
distractors: (n + alpha) / (N_c + 2 alpha), as for a binary attribute.
(n + K alpha) / (N_c + alpha).
n / (N_c + K alpha).

cards.question: For a continuous attribute, how does Naive Bayes model p(x_j = x | y = c) with the robust estimate?
cards.answer: A normal density N(x | mu_{j|c}, sigma^2 = (sigma_{j|c} + alpha)^2), using the class mean and standard deviation of that attribute.
distractors: A Bernoulli distribution with parameter equal to the class mean.
A normal density with the covariance matrix of all attributes together.
A uniform density over the range of the attribute in class c.

cards.question: Why do we add a small number alpha to the counts in Naive Bayes?
cards.answer: To avoid zero estimated probabilities when a value never occurs in a class, since one zero factor would force the whole product to zero.
distractors: To make the class priors sum to more than 1.
To convert continuous attributes into binary ones.
To ensure the attributes become independent.

cards.question: How should the smoothing parameter alpha be selected?
cards.answer: Using cross-validation.
distractors: Always set it to the number of attributes M.
Set it to the training-set accuracy.
Set it to the class prior of the majority class.

cards.question: In a binary attribute within a class of N_c = 10 observations, the value 1 never occurs. With alpha = 1, what is the smoothed estimate of p(x_j = 1 | y = c)?
A categorical attribute with K = 3 categories takes category k in 2 of the N_c = 8 observations of class c. With alpha = 1, what is the smoothed estimate?
How does Bayesian classification with the multivariate normal distribution work?
cards.answer: Fit a normal distribution to each class by computing the class mean and covariance, then classify using P(y=c|x) = P(x|y=c)P(y=c) / sum over c' of P(x|y=c')P(y=c').
distractors: Fit one normal distribution to all the data, and classify by the nearest class mean.
Fit a normal distribution only to the largest class, and classify others as outliers.
Compute the class mean only, assuming the covariance matrix is zero.

cards.question: For male and female height/weight data, a Gaussian is fit to each class. What differs between the two fitted densities?
cards.answer: Each class has its own mean vector and covariance matrix (its own location, spread and orientation).
distractors: Only the mean differs; the covariance matrix is shared and fixed to the identity.
Only the prior differs; the densities are identical.
They have the same mean but different class labels.

cards.question: What does the Naive Bayes independence assumption correspond to in the parameters of a multivariate normal class model?
cards.answer: The covariances between different attributes are zero, so the covariance matrix is diagonal and p(x1, x2) factorizes into p(x1) p(x2).
distractors: The mean vector is zero for every class.
The covariance matrix is the identity matrix for all classes.
The covariance matrix is not symmetric.

cards.question: How is precision defined for a classifier?
cards.answer: The number of true positives divided by the number of observations predicted positive.
distractors: The number of true positives divided by the number of actual positives.
The number of correct predictions divided by the total number of observations.
The number of false positives divided by the number of actual negatives.

cards.question: How is recall defined for a classifier?
cards.answer: The number of true positives divided by the number of actual positives.
distractors: The number of true positives divided by the number predicted positive.
The number of true negatives divided by the number of actual negatives.
The number of false negatives divided by the number of actual positives.

cards.question: A test set has 20 positives. Classifier 1 predicts 54 positives, 18 correct. Classifier 2 predicts 16 positives, 14 correct. What are the precision and recall of each?
cards.answer: Classifier 1: precision 1/3, recall 9/10. Classifier 2: precision 7/8, recall 7/10.
distractors: Classifier 1: precision 2/3, recall 7/10. Classifier 2: precision 1/3, recall 1/3.
Classifier 1: precision 1/3, recall 9/10. Classifier 2: precision 2/3, recall 9/10.
Classifier 1: precision 9/10, recall 1/3. Classifier 2: precision 7/10, recall 7/8.

cards.question: If the objective is to detect credit-card fraud (positive = fraud) and you want to miss few fraudulent transactions, which classifier from the previous example is preferable and why?
cards.answer: Classifier 1, because it has the higher recall (9/10 versus 7/10), meaning fewer missed frauds (fewer false negatives).
distractors: Classifier 2, because its precision of 7/8 means it misses fewer frauds.
Classifier 2, because it makes fewer positive predictions overall.
Neither, because precision and recall cannot be compared between classifiers.
